new.title: Find Barlach's figures and a Tintoretto at St. Katharinen
new.desc: Lübeck's only surviving monastery church was built for the Franciscans, who arrived in 1225. In the niches of the west front stand three brick figures by Ernst Barlach, hidden in 1936 to save them from being seized as degenerate art, with six more added by Gerhard Marcks after the war. Inside hangs The Raising of Lazarus from 1576, the only Tintoretto in northern Europe.
new.tip: The facade figures can be seen from Königstraße at any time for free. The interior is a museum church that usually opens only Thursday to Sunday afternoons from April to mid October.

new.title: Step into a merchant's salon at the Behnhaus
new.desc: This town house on Königstraße was built in 1783 and is one of the grandest classicist merchant homes in the old town. Today it shows 19th century and early modern painting, from Caspar David Friedrich to Edvard Munch, with a strong group of works by the Lübeck-born Nazarene Friedrich Overbeck.
new.tip: The Behnhaus has reopened after its renovation, while work on the neighbouring Drägerhaus is only starting, so check which rooms are open. Do not miss the garden behind the house with its sculptures.

new.title: Visit St. Aegidien, the craftsmen's little church
new.desc: St. Aegidien is the smallest and most easterly of the old town's churches, first mentioned in 1227. It was the parish of the craftsmen who lived on the slope down to the Wakenitz, and its coat of arms carries a T for Tilgenkark, the Low German name of the church.
new.tip: Combine it with a wander through the quiet lanes around the Aegidienhof, a part of the old town most visitors never reach.

new.title: Stand under a sperm whale beside the cathedral
new.desc: The Museum für Natur und Umwelt first opened in 1893 and now sits right next to the cathedral, joined to it by a cloister. A sperm whale skeleton hangs in the courtyard, and inside are fossil baleen whales from the Miocene that were dug out of a gravel pit at Groß Pampau.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays. The section on the Wakenitz, the Trave and the Bay of Lübeck is the one that makes sense of the landscape you see around town.
new.q: Museum für Natur und Umwelt, Musterbahn 8, Lübeck

new.title: See Lübeck's industrial past in Herrenwyk
new.desc: This small museum fills the former company store of the Lübeck blast furnace works, in the middle of the workers' settlement of Herrenwyk. It tells of work at the furnaces, life in the colony, forced labour in the Second World War and the rise and fall of the Flender shipyard, with a grocer's shop, a working forge and a steam hammer.
new.tip: It opens only on Friday afternoons and at weekends. Herrenwyk lies in Kücknitz on the way to Travemünde, so it fits well into a trip to the coast.

new.title: Walk past the thatched fishermen's houses of Gothmund
new.desc: Gothmund is a tiny fishing settlement on the Trave between Lübeck and Travemünde, first mentioned in 1502. A footpath leads past a row of reed-thatched fishermen's cottages, with a little natural harbour hidden behind a belt of reeds. The village has been a listed ensemble since 2018.
new.tip: People live here, so stay on the path and keep your voice down. The walk joins up nicely with the Schellbruch nature reserve next door.

new.title: Go birdwatching in the Schellbruch lagoons
new.desc: The Schellbruch is a nature reserve of brackish lagoons, reed beds and wet meadows on the lower Trave. More than 200 bird species have been recorded here, almost 100 of them breeding. In the 1970s the area was to be filled in for the port, until citizens of Lübeck stopped the plan.
new.tip: Follow the Treidelstieg, the old towpath that separates the lagoons from the river. Bring binoculars and come early in the morning.

new.title: Watch an arthouse film at Kino Koki
new.desc: The Koki is Lübeck's communal cinema, a small independent house on Mengstraße run by an association. It shows arthouse films, documentaries and themed series such as Italian film weeks, usually with two screenings an evening.
new.tip: Many films run in the original language with subtitles, which the programme marks. Seats are few, so reserve for festival series.

new.title: Drink the house beer at Im alten Zolln
new.desc: This pub on Mühlenstraße has been pouring since 1589 and calls itself the oldest inn in Lübeck. Its old name was De olde Tollbode, after the customs officer who lived here. It serves hearty home cooking, a dark top-fermented house beer and regular live music.
new.tip: It opens in the late afternoon from Tuesday to Saturday and stays shut on Sunday and Monday. In fine weather take a table on the terrace.

new.title: Try marzipan tea at the Speicher-Rösterei
new.desc: At the harbour end of Beckergrube, a brick warehouse from 1871 houses a café that roasts its own coffee. The menu leans on the local speciality: marzipan tea, marzipan cake and marzipan ice cream, alongside nougat and chocolate.
new.tip: Ask for a table on the terrace facing the old town harbour. It is open every day until early evening.

new.title: Have cake under the thatch at Landschätzchen
new.desc: The Benett family has run this garden café in Israelsdorf, on the wooded northern edge of Lübeck, for more than 25 years. It serves home-made cream cakes, tray bakes and ice cream sundaes, and sells game from local hunts.
new.tip: In season it opens on Saturday and Sunday afternoons only, and it closes in bad weather. It makes a good stop after a walk in the Schellbruch or to Gothmund.

new.title: Eat cake in a beach chair at Hofcafé Bisdorf
new.desc: In the village of Bisdorf, in the middle of Fehmarn, this farm café has baked all its cakes fresh every day for 25 years. In summer you sit in hooded beach chairs in the sheltered farmyard, and on cool days indoors at long tables.
new.tip: It opens daily in the afternoon during the season, which ends in late October. You cannot reserve, so just turn up, and dogs are welcome.

new.title: Buy farm cheese and bread at Hof Klostersee
new.desc: Hof Klostersee near Cismar has been farmed biodynamically since 1987 and is owned by a non-profit association. The farm runs its own dairy and bakery, and the farm shop in the yard sells its cheese, bread, meat and sausage. A garden café looks out over the working farm.
new.tip: The shop and café close on Sundays and public holidays. Behind the farm lies the Kellenhusen forest with its ancient oaks, and the beach is under three kilometres away.

new.title: Taste wine from Holstein at the Ingenhof
new.desc: The Ingenhof at Malkwitz near Malente is a fruit farm that also grows wine, a rarity this far north. Its field café among the vines and orchards serves home-made strawberry cake and savoury snacks with a glass of the farm's own wine, such as its Solaris.
new.tip: The farm runs vineyard tours with a tasting, and in summer you can pick your own strawberries and raspberries. Check the café season on the farm's website before you drive out.

new.title: Lick farm-made ice cream at Hof Steffens
new.desc: On their dairy farm at Langendamm near Ahrensbök, the Steffens family makes ice cream by hand from the milk and cream of their own cows. The farm café looks out over the fields, and the shop sells ice cream, yoghurt, milk, cheese and jam.
new.tip: The café opens at weekends from Easter to October, while the farm shop is open most of the year. Card payment only works for larger amounts, so bring cash.

new.title: Have coffee among the cows at Gut Wulfsdorf
new.desc: Gut Wulfsdorf on the edge of Ahrensburg is a large biodynamic farm with a farm shop, a wood-oven bakery, a butcher and an ice cream hut. At the farm shop café the soundtrack is cows, sheep, hens and the odd passing tractor.
new.tip: The shop and café are open Monday to Saturday and closed on Sundays. Ask for the bread of the month from the wood oven.

new.title: Climb the tower on the Bungsberg, the roof of the north
new.desc: At 167.4 metres the Bungsberg is the highest point in Schleswig-Holstein. Near the top stands the Elisabethturm, a 22-metre octagonal tower of granite blocks built in 1863 and 1864 by the Grand Duke of Oldenburg and named after his wife. It reopened to visitors in 2017 after a long restoration.
new.tip: The Schwentine, one of the longest rivers in the state, rises on the slope of the hill. On a clear day the view reaches the Baltic.

new.title: Tour Schloss Reinbek, a Dutch Renaissance palace
new.desc: Schloss Reinbek was built from 1572 to 1576 for Duke Adolf I of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorf, with Dutch craftsmen on the site. The three brick wings with sandstone trim were restored between 1977 and 1987, and the palace is now the town's arts centre, with painted beam ceilings, exhibitions and concerts.
new.tip: The palace sits in a park of old trees on the mill pond. The attic, called the Krummspanner, holds changing exhibitions and a room on the town's history.

new.title: Find the monks' manor house at Nütschau
new.desc: The Benedictine priory of St. Ansgar in Travenbrück, near Bad Oldesloe, grew around a small moated manor that the humanist Heinrich Rantzau began in 1577. The house passed through 28 owners before the church bought it in 1951 and monks from Gerleve Abbey moved in.
new.tip: This is a working monastery, so keep it quiet. Look up the service times and the guest house on the priory's website if you want more than a look from outside.

new.title: Squeeze through submarine U 11 on Fehmarn
new.desc: U 11 served in the German navy from 1968 and covered almost 178,000 nautical miles before it was retired in 2003. Since 2005 the boat has been a museum in the harbour of Burgstaaken on Fehmarn, where you can walk through its narrow interior.
new.tip: The hatches are low and the gangways tight, so leave big bags behind. Look for the second hull it was given when it was turned into a practice target boat.

new.title: Watch migrating birds from the hides at Wallnau
new.desc: On the west coast of Fehmarn, the Wallnau reserve covers about 297 hectares of ponds, reed beds, meadows and shoreline. More than 270 bird species rest here on migration and around 100 breed, among them red-necked grebes and little terns. The conservation group NABU looks after the reserve and runs its visitor centre.
new.tip: Spring and autumn migration bring the biggest numbers. Galloway cattle graze the meadows, so you may see them from the paths too.

new.title: Meet the owls at Vogelpark Niendorf
new.desc: This bird park in Niendorf, founded in 1973, keeps around 1,000 birds of 250 species in a reed landscape beside the Aalbeek valley. Its owl collection is one of the largest in the world, and there are storks, pelicans, flamingos, toucans and hornbills too.
new.tip: The paths are step-free and work well with a pushchair or wheelchair. The park is a short walk from Niendorf's fishing harbour.

new.title: Circle the Ukleisee through the beech woods
new.desc: The Ukleisee near Eutin is a kettle lake left behind by the last ice age, with a shoreline of just over three kilometres that a circular path follows. Near the water stands a little hunting lodge built in 1776 for the Dukes of Oldenburg, now used for concerts.
new.tip: Start in Sielbeck and allow about an hour for the loop. Traces of a medieval Slavic rampart can still be made out on the shore.

new.title: Hike the Hahnheide to the Langer Otto tower
new.desc: The Hahnheide east of Trittau is a hilly forest of about 1,400 hectares, protected since 1938. On the Großer Hahnheider Berg stands a 27-metre wooden lookout tower nicknamed Langer Otto after a former mayor, rebuilt in 2001.
new.tip: The hill next door, the Kleiner Hahnheider Berg, is oddly the higher of the two by about a metre. Wear proper shoes, as the forest tracks get muddy.

new.title: Swim in the clear water of the Großensee
new.desc: The Großensee in southern Stormarn is a glacial lake of 73 hectares, fed mostly by groundwater and up to 16 metres deep. It has belonged to the city of Hamburg since the 1920s. There is a lido at the southern end in the village of Großensee and a free bathing beach at the northern end near Lütjensee.
new.tip: A path of about six kilometres loops around the lake if you would rather walk. On hot weekends come early, as parking fills quickly.
